text: This lesson closes chapter one with two measurements that describe how fast a system actually feels: latency and throughput. They sound similar, but improving one doesn't automatically improve the other.

Latency is the time for a single request to complete, start to finish. Throughput is how many requests a system can process per unit time, often per second. They trade off: batching small requests together raises throughput, because processing in bulk is more efficient, but it raises the latency of each individual request, since some of them now wait for the batch to fill. Neither is universally better — it depends on whether you're serving live users or doing bulk background work.

In a distributed system, the average response time can be misleading, which is why tail latency matters — p99, the time 99% of requests beat, or p999 for an even stricter bar. Here's why it matters so much: a request that fans out to twenty downstream services can only be as fast as the slowest of those twenty. Even if each one is slow just one percent of the time, there's a real chance one of twenty is in its slow moment on any given request, dragging the whole thing down.

On a single machine, a function call is effectively instant. In a distributed system, every call to another machine crosses a network, and that trip takes real time a single-machine program never paid. A request fanning out to five services pays for five network round trips before a response can even be assembled — latency that only exists because the system is distributed.
That closes chapter one: distributed systems, availability, scalability, reliability, and now latency and throughput. Chapter two opens with lesson six: asynchronous systems.
